wstep: This card describes the Colorado State University Extension recipe for peach pickles: small peeled peaches cooked in a spiced vinegar and sugar syrup, hot packed into pint jars and processed in a boiling-water bath.

ostrzezenia.tekst: Process only pint jars and only up to 10000 ft (up to 3000 m): CSU gives times only for pint jars, no time for quart jars and no time above 10000 ft.
Use yellow-flesh peaches: the natural pH of some white peaches can be above 4.6, and NCHFP has no researched acidification procedure for safe boiling-water canning of white-flesh peaches.

akapity: The recipe uses peeled peaches, small to medium size, 1 to 1 1/2 inches (about 2.5–3.8 cm) in diameter.
The FDA list gives peaches a pH of about 3.30–4.05.
The natural pH of some white peaches can be above 4.6, which makes them a low-acid food for canning.
NCHFP has no pressure process and no researched acidification for them, and recommends freezing white-flesh peaches instead.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): the CSU recipe names only peaches, so this card does not cover nectarines.

sekcje.naglowek: Why you must not change the recipe
akapity: The whole product must contain a minimum, uniform level of acid so that botulism bacteria cannot grow.
Do not change the proportions of vinegar, fruit and water and do not use vinegar of unknown acidity; use only recipes with tested proportions.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): do not change the amounts of vinegar or peaches and do not add other fruit or vegetables; the recipe is tested only in the proportions given.
White distilled vinegar and cider vinegar of 5% acidity are recommended for pickles.

JarAtlas rule (cautious, for readers outside the USA): use white distilled (spirit) vinegar or cider vinegar labelled 5% or 6% acidity; do not use 10% vinegar and do not dilute it with water to make 5% vinegar; add only the water the recipe lists.
A US cup holds about 237 ml.

For about 6 pint jars CSU lists 8 pounds (about 3.6 kg) of peeled peaches, 1/2 teaspoon of ascorbic acid, 6 3/4 cups of sugar, 4 cinnamon sticks 2 inches long, 2 tablespoons of whole cloves (crushed), 1 tablespoon of ginger and 1 quart (about 946 ml) of vinegar of 5% acidity.
To keep the peeled peaches from darkening, drop them into a cold solution of 1/2 teaspoon of ascorbic acid per 2 quarts of water.
Dissolve the sugar in the vinegar in a saucepot, heat it, boil for 5 minutes and skim.
Add the spices tied in cheesecloth.
Drain the peaches and cook them in the boiling syrup until they can be pierced with a fork but are not soft.
Let the peaches stand in the syrup overnight in the refrigerator.
Bring them to a boil again before packing them into hot jars.
Fill hot jars with the peaches, leaving 1/2 inch (about 1.3 cm) of headspace, and cover them with syrup, leaving 1/2 inch of headspace.
Close the jars with two-piece canning lids and process them in a boiling-water bath.
Up to 1000 ft (up to 300 m) process pint jars for 20 minutes.
Above 1000 ft the food may spoil if the time is not increased.
At 1001–3000 ft (above 300 m up to 900 m) process them for 25 minutes.
At 3001–6000 ft (above 900 m up to 1800 m) process them for 30 minutes.
At 6001–10000 ft (above 1800 m up to 3000 m) process them for 35 minutes.
Above 10000 ft (above 3000 m) CSU gives no time, so this card does not cover canning at that elevation.
The card converts feet to metres and rounds the limits down, towards the longer time: 1000 ft becomes 300 m, 3000 ft becomes 900 m and 6000 ft becomes 1800 m.
10000 ft (3048 m) becomes 3000 m, so the range without a time is wider than in the source.
Shortening the time or cooling jars in cold water can also lead to spoilage.
CSU gives times only for pint jars, not for quart jars.
JarAtlas rule (NCHFP does not test metric jars): a pint holds about 473 ml, so a 0.5 l jar has no tested time in this recipe; use jars of up to 473 ml.
When you take the hot jars out of the canner, do not retighten the lids or bands; this can cut through the gasket and cause seal failures.

Cool the jars at room temperature for 12 to 24 hours, then remove only the screw bands (the metal rings of two-piece lids), leaving the flat lids on the jars, and test the seal: press the middle of the lid, and if it springs up when you release it, the jar is not sealed.

NCHFP calls Mason-type canning jars with self-sealing two-piece lids (a flat lid and a screw band) the best choice, and this seal test and the method on this card assume them; NCHFP does not recommend other commercial jars whose mouths cannot be sealed with two-piece canning lids for canning any food at home.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): use this card only with jars that take two-piece canning lids; it gives no method for twist-off jars or jars with glass lids, so do not use them for this recipe.
A sealed lid is concave, curved down slightly in the centre; if the centre is flat or bulging, the jar may not be sealed.
If a jar has not sealed at this check, keep it in the refrigerator and eat it within several days.

Store sealed jars in a clean, cool, dark, dry place, not above 95 °F (35 °C) and not near hot pipes, a stove or a furnace, in an uninsulated attic or in direct sunlight; in such conditions the food may spoil.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): keep an opened jar in the refrigerator and use it within 1 week.
Before using a stored jar, check that the lid is tight and holds a vacuum: a good seal has a concave centre.
Look for streaks of dried food running from the top of the jar, rising air bubbles and unnatural colour.
When opening the jar, check for an unnatural smell, spurting liquid and cotton-like mould on the food or under the lid.
Do not taste food from a jar with an unsealed lid or with signs of spoilage.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): throw out such a jar.
